assistant.note: The extension's one contributed color, dearReviewer.assistantForeground, defaulting to charts.purple. The rule and cat of the Assistant's Hand, and its Findings (ADR 0031).

finding.note: Gutter icons can't take a theme color: extension/media/finding-cat.svg and finding-bar.svg (#b180d7, dark) and finding-cat-light.svg and finding-bar-light.svg (#652d90, light) carry charts.purple's defaults.

extensions.colorNote: Every color is a VS Code theme variable, so no tonal ramps exist; the theme supplies all values. previewValue is VS Code's Dark Modern default, for previews outside the editor only.

masthead-title.purpose: The Change overview's title, the one large line in Dear Reviewer (The Masthead Rule). Steps down to 1.3em in a column 640px or narrower.

masthead-facts.purpose: The overview's facts line under its title: size, additions and deletions, and check health, in tabular numerals.

headline.purpose: Section headings in a panel, such as Your Review.

section-label.purpose: The overview's sections below the masthead (Checks, the history, the Reading Order), headed as the editor heads its own views. A SHA in one keeps its case.

body.purpose: Messages, timeline bodies and rendered Markdown.

label.purpose: Muted metadata: dates, the pull-request reference, the Claude login, steps.

status.purpose: Check status pills and selection chips.

code.purpose: Editor font for SHAs, paths, step subjects and Markdown code.

motion.name: progress
motion.value: 2px of --vscode-progressBar-background sliding along the top edge, shown only after 300ms; still across the width under reduced motion, from the system or the editor
motion.purpose: Loading, in every webview; the only motion outside the Code Flow.

motion.name: ease-out
motion.purpose: The Code Flow's glides: symbols the call map keeps, moving to their new places.

motion.name: glide
motion.purpose: A kept symbol of the call map moving to its new place when the map draws other symbols.

motion.name: enter
motion.value: 220ms ease-out fade; columns 60ms apart on a first draw, at most 240ms
motion.purpose: New symbols and calls of the call map arriving where they land, calls after both their ends.

motion.name: exit
motion.purpose: Symbols and calls the call map drops, fading where they were.

motion.name: trace
motion.value: 640ms: a 2px --vscode-editor-foreground line drawn along the arrow over the first 60% (cubic-bezier(0.3, 0, 0.2, 1)), then faded
motion.purpose: Ink running once along a selected symbol's calls, or down a new swimlane trace, rows at most 45ms apart and 360ms in all.

motion.name: reduced
motion.purpose: Every Code Flow motion under reduced motion, from the system or the editor's own setting.

narrative.overview:
The Change's code is the page, and the code lives only in the editor. Dear Reviewer writes in the margin beside it: the timeline, the Assistant's replies and the Findings list are notes about the code, never a second copy of it (ADR 0012). A margin note is in the reader's own hand and the book's own ink. Every surface takes its color, type and controls from the active VS Code theme, and must look right in light, dark and high-contrast themes without a single theme-specific rule.

The system has almost nothing of its own on purpose. Native UI comes first: tree views, comment threads, gutter decorations, codicons, quick picks and the status bar. The four webviews, each Change's overview, the Dashboard, the Assistant's view and the Code Flow, exist only where no native view fits, and they behave like editor panels: compact, text-led, flat, divided by hairlines, readable for a whole working day. Density is the editor's density. A Reviewer who glances from the diff to the margin should notice the content, not the change of world.

Rejected on sight: the GitHub Pull Requests extension's webviews, which are slow, custom-styled review pages that look wrong next to VSCodium, and branded AI chat panels with gradients, glows, sparkle motifs or a face for the bot. The Assistant is not a character, but it writes in a hand of its own: a rule down the margin of what it says, headed by the reading cat and its name, in the one color the extension adds (ADR 0031).
keyCharacteristics: Every color is a `--vscode-*` theme variable; the extension adds one, the Assistant's, which a theme can set.
Type is the workbench font for prose and the editor font for anything code-shaped.
Flat surfaces, 1px hairlines and sticky bars on the editor background.
Controls copy VS Code's own: 2px corners, theme button colors, no flourish.
Code shows in webviews only as plain quoted text; navigation happens in the editor.

rules.name: The Borrowed Ink Rule
rules.body: No literal color values in any surface. If a role has no `--vscode-*` variable, pick the nearest semantic one and give it a fallback inside `var()`; never write a hex value. The one exception is an image the editor draws that can't take a theme color, such as a gutter icon: give it light and dark variants in the theme color's default values.

rules.name: The Semantic Hue Rule
rules.body: Hue means state, never decoration: green for passed, red for failed or a problem, the Assistant's color for what the Assistant says, Findings included, and the warning color for a Claude login billed per token. Nothing is colored only to look nice.

rules.name: The Two Fonts Rule
rules.body: The workbench font for words, the editor font for anything a Reviewer might paste into a terminal or search for in the code. No third family, no web fonts.

rules.name: The Relative Size Rule
rules.body: Sizes are `em` multiples of the theme size, so a Reviewer's zoom and font settings carry through.

rules.name: The Masthead Rule
rules.body: Only the overview's masthead, its title and facts line, is set larger than the theme size; nothing else in Dear Reviewer is. It is what makes the overview recognizably Dear Reviewer's without a color or font of its own: scale at the top, editor-plain below. Everything under the masthead reads at body size or smaller, so the masthead stays the one peak.

rules.name: The Hairline Rule
rules.body: Separate with a 1px `hairline` or a theme tint, never a shadow, gradient or blur. If something needs to float, it should be native VS Code UI (a quick pick, hover or notification), not a webview layer.

rules.name: The Assistant's Hand Rule
rules.body: Wherever the Assistant speaks in a webview, its words sit behind a 2px rule in the Assistant's color, headed by the reading cat in that color and "Assistant" in `foreground`, at label size and semibold. The hand has no fill, so the Reviewer's filled messages stay the main flow. Nothing else uses its color or its cat, so a Reviewer can tell the Assistant's words from the Reviewer's own, from GitHub's and from Dear Reviewer's at a glance; the one other rule in the overview, the result block's, takes a state color and has no cat or name. In the editor, the Finding's gutter bar is the same rule.

rules.name: The Next Step Rule
rules.body: The overview fills only the button for what comes next. While files are unviewed, that is the way in: Start at, or Next unviewed file when the take names no file. Once every file is viewed, it is Submit Review… or Write Brief…, which stays in the same place in the sticky header throughout and is secondary until then. It is secondary again while the Submit step is open, whose own Submit Review is the filled one, and once a Review covers the head with no Comments pending, when there is nothing to finish. Next unviewed file, Ask the Assistant and the finishing button show their key beside the label, in the editor font and the Reviewer's own notation (`Ctrl+Alt+R N`, or `⌃⌥R N` on a Mac), which isn't part of the name a screen reader gives the button; tooltips give it too. The Dashboard follows the same rule across all the Reviewer's Changes (see Dashboard).

rules.name: The Steady Focus Rule
rules.body: An update never moves the Reviewer's focus. The webviews rebuild only what changed, such as the reply being written or a history that loaded again, and if a rebuilt element had the focus, it goes to the element in the same place. When the focused element hides or is disabled, such as Stop once a reply ends or the last selection chip removed, the focus goes to the element in the same place, else the panel's default (the Assistant's message box), else the nearest one before it; never to the page. A button that waits on the extension, such as Submit Review while GitHub takes the Review, is `aria-disabled` rather than disabled, so it keeps the focus.

rules.name: The One Paragraph Rule
rules.body: The Assistant's take is at most three sentences and ends by naming where to start. The overview enforces it: anything longer waits behind Show all.

rules.name: The Breathing Room Rule
rules.body: Opening a Change shows one thing. Nothing opens beside the overview, below it or behind it until the Reviewer asks.

dos: **Do** take every color from a `--vscode-*` variable, with a fallback inside `var()` when the theme might not define it, as in `var(--vscode-input-border, transparent)`.
**Do** reach for native UI first (tree views, comment threads, decorations, quick picks, status bar) and add a webview only when an ADR says why none fits.

**Do** put styles every webview uses in `sharedStyles` in `extension/src/markdownPanel.ts`, and the overview's page styles (header, buttons, facts line, status pills, rows) in `pageStyles` in `extension/src/timeline/panel.ts`, never a copy in each panel.
**Do** give every interactive element a visible `:focus-visible` outline in `focus`, and make links in rendered Markdown reachable with Tab and Enter.

**Do** show loading with VS Code's progress bar, the only motion in Dear Reviewer outside the Code Flow (see Navigation): 2px of `progressBar-background` sliding along the top, appearing only after 300ms so a quick load doesn't flash. Each webview draws it (`.progress` in `sharedStyles`) along its top edge, right under the view's header: the Dashboard while the Inbox loads, on Refresh too, and the overview while its timeline loads. With reduced motion, from the system or from the editor's own setting, it holds still across the width, with no animation at all. The muted loading line stays beside it, for screen readers and for a first load with nothing else to show.

**Do** announce status to screen readers: `role="status"` for loading and working lines, `role="alert"` for the problem banner, and a visually hidden status line for changes that are otherwise only visual, such as a reply finishing. Set a live region's text only when it changes (`setText` in `sharedScript`), or every update speaks it again.
**Do** keep the focus through updates with `keepFocus` in `sharedScript`, and build only the parts of a webview that changed.

**Do** give every element that has a fill a theme border or outline that high-contrast themes draw: `--vscode-button-border` on buttons, `--vscode-contrastBorder` on tints such as the Reviewer's message and the avatar disc.
**Do** color placeholders with `--vscode-input-placeholderForeground`; the browser's default gray fails contrast on dark themes.
**Do** check every webview change in a light, a dark and a high-contrast theme in VSCodium.
**Do** size type in `em` from the theme size, and use the editor font for SHAs, paths and code.
donts: **Don't** show the Change's code as code in a webview: no files, diffs, hunks, line numbers or syntax highlighting (ADR 0012).
**Don't** write a literal color, except in an editor-drawn image that can't take a theme color, and then only the theme color's default values.
**Don't** use shadows, gradients, blur or glow.
**Don't** brand the Assistant beyond its Hand: no avatar, mascot, face, fill, gradient, glow or sparkle motif. Its marks are the reading cat, its name, its rule and its color, and nothing else.
**Don't** build custom-styled review pages in the manner of the GitHub Pull Requests extension's webviews.
**Don't** load web fonts or set absolute font sizes.
